slides.title: Executive summary

paragraphs.text: Executive summary
Parcelbird should not launch Parcelbird Now in 2027; it should fund the software business, which can reach breakeven within today's cash
Quick commerce is growing fast, but its operators lose money on the average order and are retreating
–	US sales grew 2.8 times in 2022–25, yet both incumbents lose money on the average order
At the median customer site each order would lose $6.17; only the founders' plan makes money
–	Even the best observed level on every input would lose $1.76 per order
–	The plan needs four inputs beyond the best any site has reached
Customers do not stay long enough to repay what it costs to acquire them
–	Only 22% of pop-up customers still order in month three, and each needs about 28 months to repay
The launch breaks the board's runway rule even on plan, and its downside exceeds all the cash
–	Runway at month 18 would be about 6 months, half the 12-month floor
–	Nine stores at the median would lose about $18M a year, against $12.0M of cash
Scaling the software is the better use of the cash; four conditions would justify revisiting the launch
–	The 37-grocer pipeline is worth $3.6M of ARR, against $4.1M today
–	The software would break even at about $11M of ARR, using about $6.6M of cash
